title: The Plain of Troy as the Iliad Lays It Out

layers.note: The water the ships are hauled out of: the Achaeans lie on the Hellespont (Il. 7.86, 23.2), on the grey sea's beach, θῖν' ἔφ' ἁλὸς πολιῆς (14.31).

The ground itself. The Achaeans pour out from the ships and the huts ἐς πεδίον … Σκαμάνδριον and take their stand μυρίοι in the flowery Scamandrian meadow (Il. 2.464-68) — everything between the camp and the city. Drawn as a lettering zone and nothing more, because the plain is not a place on this sheet: it is the sheet. That is also why it takes no anchor — a pin would put the plain at one point of itself — and why a scene set here is framed by the whole plate, unzoomed.

sources.cite: Strabo. Geography 13.1.34.

layers.note: The camp fills the whole long mouth of the shore, ἠϊόνος στόμα μακρόν, ὅσον συνεέργαθον ἄκραι (Il. 14.36) — the beach could not hold the ships in one line, so they were hauled up in tiers, προκρόσσας (14.35). The plate takes Pope's 1716 viewpoint, sea at the bottom and Troy at the top, because that is where the poet stands. The camp's two ends are named by who holds them and never by a hand: Ajax's end and Achilles' end, ἔσχατα (8.222-26 = 11.5-9).

layers.note: The city stands at the head of the plain, its gates on the side that faces the fighting.
Ida closes the horizon behind Troy, as it does on Pope's plate. From its ridges run the rivers Poseidon and Apollo will turn against the Achaean wall (Il. 12.19-22).

One of the two headlands that close the beach, ὅσον συνεέργαθον ἄκραι (Il. 14.36). Deliberately unnamed: Sigeion and Rhoiteion are Strabo's names for these promontories and neither occurs anywhere in the Iliad.
The far headland. The poem gives the pair a function — they measure the camp's length — and no names.
The citadel rises behind the city; Ares shouts down to the Trojans ἀκροτάτης πόλιος, from the topmost point of it (Il. 20.52).

The river runs down one flank of the plain and reaches the sea beyond that end of the ships — the flank the Simoeis does not hold. Which flank that is in the ground is a question for the geographic sheet, and the one line that ties a hand to a physical feature, μάχης ἐπ' ἀριστερὰ … ὄχθας πὰρ ποταμοῖο Σκαμάνδρου (Il. 11.498-99), hands it to a river position nobody has. Its head on this plate is the pair of springs under Troy's wall, because that is where the poem puts it: πηγαὶ δοιαὶ ἀναΐσσουσι Σκαμάνδρου δινήεντος (Il. 22.147-48) — a hydrography the ground cannot support, which is exactly why it belongs to this register and not to the geographic plate.

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Troy: A Study in Homeric Geography. London: Macmillan, 1912.

layers.note: The Simoeis comes down the other flank. The two rivers are drawn to separate mouths: the poem does speak of them joining their streams (Il. 5.774), and Pope drew the confluence, but Leaf 1912 showed no such junction exists, and a schematic plate should not multiply the errors it inherits.

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Troy: A Study in Homeric Geography. London: Macmillan, 1912.

layers.note: The beach, αἰγιαλός, broad and still too narrow to take all the ships in one line (Il. 14.33-34). Its curve here is compositional, not surveyed — the reconstructed Bronze Age shoreline belongs to the geographic plate.
The wall of Troy, with its gates set on the arc that faces the plain. Andromache runs along it to the great tower when she hears the Trojans are being worn down (Il. 6.386-88).

The high heaped-up wall the Trojans and Pallas Athene made for Heracles, so he could dodge the sea-monster as it drove him from the shore inland (Il. 20.145-48). Poseidon and the gods who favour the Achaeans take their seats on it, wrapping themselves in unbreakable cloud (20.149-50) — one half of the divine grandstand, set opposite Callicolone across the plain.
Outside the wall they dug the ditch, deep and wide and great, and planted stakes in it: ἔκτοσθεν δὲ βαθεῖαν ἐπ' αὐτῷ τάφρον ὄρυξαν (Il. 7.440-41).

The wall with its high towers, a defence for the ships and for the men (Il. 7.436-37), built at the sterns of the first-hauled rank: τεῖχος ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν ἔδειμαν (14.32). It is drawn light because the poem itself unbuilds it — Poseidon and Apollo turn the Idaean rivers against it and sweep it into the sea (12.17-24).

The wagon-road, ἀμαξιτός: Hector and Achilles run along it under the wall, past the lookout and the windy fig tree, and come to the two springs (Il. 22.145-48). Priam takes the same ground outward, driving past the great tomb of Ilos and halting at the river to water the mules (24.349-51). The waypoints are strung along it in the order the poem narrates them, which fixes their sequence and not their distances.

The chariot way into the camp, crossing ditch and wall at the end of the line where the teams come back in off the plain: Asius drives at that gate, νηῶν ἐπ' ἀριστερά, τῇ περ Ἀχαιοὶ ἐκ πεδίου νίσοντο σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφι (Il. 12.118-19), and it is there Idomeneus kills him (12.117; 13.384-88). The gates were built wide on purpose, ὄφρα δι' αὐτάων ἱππηλασίη ὁδὸς εἴη (7.438-39). Labelled by that event rather than by a hand, because whose left 12.118 means is disputed — Janko reads it from the Greek side, Hainsworth from Asius's. Drawn as a separate stretch because the poem attests both this approach and the wagon-road without ever saying they are one road.

layers.note: Ajax's end of the line. The poem divides the army in three of its own accord — ἐπὶ δεξιόφιν παντὸς στρατοῦ, ἦ ἀνὰ μέσσους, ἦ ἐπ' ἀριστερόφιν (Il. 13.308-9) — three sectors and no more, and this sheet names them by who holds them rather than by a hand, because whose left the poem's ἀριστερά is remains disputed.

sources.cite: Janko, Richard. The Iliad: A Commentary, Volume IV: Books 13–16. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994.
Hainsworth, Bryan. The Iliad: A Commentary, Volume III: Books 9–12. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

layers.note: Three receding ranks, and the rank nearest the plain is the one hauled up first: τὰς γὰρ πρώτας πεδίον δὲ εἴρυσαν (Il. 14.31-32). The camp therefore has depth and not merely length, and it is that first-hauled front rank the Trojans reach first — περὶ δ' ἔσχεθον ἄκραι νῆες ὅσαι πρῶται εἰρύατο (15.653-54). No contingent beyond the five named below is placed: the poem does not station the Catalogue along the beach, and no reconstruction that does so is defensible.

Achilles' end of the line, running out to the Myrmidon station at the far extremity. Menelaus, searching the ranks for Ajax, catches sight of him μάχης ἐπ' ἀριστερὰ πάσης (Il. 17.116) — the sector at the other end of this same line, which the poem names by a hand and this sheet names by its holder.

A steep mound in front of the city, standing apart in the plain and clear on every side, αἰπεῖα κολώνη ... περίδρομος ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα — men call it Batieia, the gods the barrow of Myrine, and there the Trojans and their allies drew up in their companies (Il. 2.811-15).

Fair Hill, beside the Simoeis (Il. 20.53), where the gods who favour Troy take their seats on the brows of it about Phoebus and Ares — οἳ δ' ἑτέρωσε καθῖζον ἐπ' ὀφρύσι Καλλικολώνης (20.151-52). Set opposite the wall of Heracles to make the two benches of the divine audience face each other across the plain.

The barrow of Ilos son of Dardanus, out in the middle of the plain: Hector takes counsel beside it at night (Il. 10.415), the rout streams past it κατὰ μέσσον πεδίον toward the city (11.166-67), wounded Agamemnon leans on its pillar (11.371-72), and Priam drives past it on the way down to the ships (24.349).

The assembly and the law-place, with the gods' altars built there — ἵνά σφ' ἀγορή τε θέμις τε ἤην, τῇ δὴ καί σφι θεῶν ἐτετεύχατο βωμοί (Il. 11.806-8). It lies at Odysseus's ships, in the middle of the camp, which is why the middle is where the army is governed.

Ajax son of Telamon at one extreme of the line: he and Achilles hauled their ships up ἔσχατα, trusting in their manhood and the strength of their hands (Il. 8.224-26 = 11.7-9). His end is set toward the promontory later called Rhoiteion, following Aristarchus and Janko, for whom the poem's ἀριστερά is always read from the Greek side — the eastern end where the Scamander ran and Telamonian Ajax lay, against the western end toward Sigeion where Achilles was stationed (Janko, Commentary IV, 130-31, on 13.675). Hainsworth reads the same phrase at 12.118 from Asius's side and swaps the two ends (Commentary III, 313-14). Neither headland is named in the Iliad, and the placement is speculative for that reason; what the sheet states is the holder, not the hand.

layers.note: Hector holds the breach where he first leapt the gates and the wall, ἔνθ' ἔσαν Αἴαντός τε νέες καὶ Πρωτεσιλάου (Il. 13.679-81), and it is Protesilaus's ship he sets alight (15.704-6). A crux the plate records rather than resolves: Patroclus, sallying from Achilles' ships at the far end of the line, is at that same stern in a single verse (16.286). Either the poet holds two incompatible pictures of the camp or the narrative compresses the distance; the drawing keeps the two extremes apart and lets the contradiction stand.

sources.cite: Cuillandre, Joseph. La droite et la gauche dans les poemes homeriques. Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1944.

layers.note: Odysseus's black ship of vast hold, ἐν μεσσάτῳ, in the very middle, so that a shout carries both ways — to the huts of Ajax at one end and to Achilles at the other (Il. 8.222-23 = 11.5-6, verbatim). The poem states the centre; it is the one position on this plate that needs no inference at all.

Nestor, rousing the camp by night, pairs Idomeneus with Ajax as the two whose ships lie furthest from his own, 'not at all near' (τῶν γὰρ νῆες ἔασιν ἑκαστάτω, οὐδὲ μάλ' ἐγγύς, Il. 10.112-13) — a statement about distance from Nestor's hut, not about which end of the line either man occupies. This placement, inboard of Achilles on the strength of the Ajax pairing alone, is the plate's own guess and is not fixed by the text.

Achilles at the other extreme (Il. 8.225-26 = 11.8-9). Pope relays the ancient reasoning from Eustathius and Spondanus: the two strongest were set to hold either end of the fleet as the most exposed to attack, and Odysseus, the ablest head, took the middle as the fitter place for counsel.

sources.cite: Pope, Alexander. The Iliad of Homer. Vol. 2. London: Bowyer for Lintott, 1716. "An Essay on Homer's Battels," 11-14.

layers.note: The Scaean Gate, where the elders of the people sit (Il. 3.145-49) and where the wagon-road leaves the city. The formula that names it names the oak in the same breath, three times over: Σκαιάς τε πύλας καὶ φηγόν (6.237 = 9.354 = 11.170).
The great tower of Ilios, beside the Scaean Gate, where Andromache goes to look out over the fighting (Il. 6.386-88).

The Dardanian Gates, the other way in: Hector makes for them again and again, hoping to get under the well-built towers (Il. 22.194-95). Set apart from the Scaean Gate because the poem treats them as a distinct entrance.
The oak, φηγός, standing just outside the Scaean Gate. Its position is fixed by the formula rather than by any description: the same line-end binds gate and tree at Il. 6.237, 9.354 and 11.170.
The lookout, σκοπιή, which Hector and Achilles pass first as they run out from under the wall along the wagon-road (Il. 22.145-46).

The windy fig tree, ἐρινεὸς ἠνεμόεις, close under the wall beside the lookout (Il. 22.145) — the weak point in the defences where the wall can be scaled (6.433-34). The poem also sets a wild fig out in the middle of the plain by Ilos's tomb (11.166-67); the two passages do not agree, and this plate follows 22.145 and marks the disagreement rather than drawing two trees.

The two fair-flowing springs, one running warm with steam rising off it as from a burning fire, the other cold as hail in summer (Il. 22.147-52), and beside them the broad fine washing-troughs of stone where the wives and daughters of the Trojans used to wash their bright clothes, in peacetime, before the sons of the Achaeans came (22.153-56).

The ford of the fair-flowing river, eddying Xanthus whom immortal Zeus begot — the one crossing between the city and the ships, and a whole verse-pair that recurs unchanged at Il. 14.433-34, 21.1-2 and 24.692-93. Placed where the wagon-road meets the river because the poem's traffic crosses there, not on any survey.
